Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports business payments to suppliers, vendors, contractors, and other businesses for commercial transactions, procurement, and supply chain payments.
Comments: No credible evidence found of a nationwide instant B2B payment scheme; however, businesses can use bank transfers/mobile money for supplier payments. Because no authoritative evidence was found describing B2B functionality in the national infrastructure, scored unknown.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check found private fintech aggregators built on mobile money rails (SerdiPay, MbiyoPay) that explicitly offer bulk/B2C business payments (salaries, commissions, supplier disbursements) and B2B collection APIs in DRC. It is unclear whether this constitutes 'the instant payment system' as scoped by this variable (i.e. the national retail switch/Mosolo or RTGS/ACH) rather than private-sector payment aggregators layered on mobile money. Evidence is suggestive but not conclusive enough to confidently move off Unknown; flagged for human review rather than guessed.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: No specific, payments-focused consumer protection framework (covering issues like error resolution, chargebacks, standardized dispute resolution for digital payments) was found for DR Congo in the reviewed sources; searches included the 2023 Digital Code summaries and BCC/NPS materials.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced an authoritative source (UNCDF/Migrant Money regional policy diagnostic, April 2025), so this row was moved to the full verification path. That source states explicitly there is no dedicated financial/payments consumer protection law in DRC, but that Instruction No. 39 obliges credit institutions and microfinance institutions to manage customer complaints through defined redressal mechanisms — i.e. sector-specific rather than comprehensive coverage. This matches 'Partial' (2) on the scale rather than 'No' (1) or 'Yes' (3). Score changed from 0/Unknown to 2/Partial on this evidence.
revised_comments: Consumer protection for digital payments in DR Congo is governed only partially: there is no dedicated, comprehensive law on payment consumer protection, but Instruction No. 39 to credit institutions and microfinance institutions establishes complaint-handling and redressal mechanisms specific to banks and MFIs. Broader gaps remain around standardised disclosure, fee transparency and dispute resolution across all payment service providers, including mobile money operators.

Definition: Percentage of the adult population (15+ years) who have made at least one digital payment transaction through the instant payment system in the past 90 days, indicating active usage rather than just account ownership.
Comments: No recent, nationally representative % of adults actively using digital payments located in the gathered sources for DR Congo. The Global Findex landing page did not provide country figures and available IMF material with DRC figures was not fully extracted/verified in this run, so scored unknown.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced authoritative sources, so this row was moved to the full verification path. A GSMA-cited report puts 90-day active mobile money subscriptions at 24.45 million as of June 2024 (a 45% penetration rate); a separate CAT/UNCDF feasibility analysis (Aug 2025, citing Q4 2024 data) records 29 million active mobile money users, equivalent to 30.5% of the Congolese population; and an IMF paper records 22% of Congolese individuals making or receiving a digital payment in the prior year. All three independent estimates converge on the 20-49% band even though they differ in exact percentage and precise denominator (adult population vs total population, 90-day vs 12-month windows). Given this convergence, the row is scored 2 (20-49%) rather than left Unknown, though the exact figure carries medium rather than high confidence due to definitional differences across sources.
revised_comments: Around a fifth to just under half of Congolese adults are estimated to have made a digital payment in the recent past, depending on measurement window and source. GSMA-linked data records 24.45 million 90-day active mobile money subscriptions as of June 2024 (a stated 45% penetration rate); a 2025 UNCDF-affiliated feasibility study citing Q4 2024 data records 29 million active mobile money users nationally (30.5% of the population); and IMF analysis found 22% of individuals reported making or receiving a digital payment in the previous year. Mobile money, rather than bank-based instant payments, is the dominant digital payment channel, with usage skewed towards urban areas and men.

revision_notes: A light check found ongoing reform activity but no quantified percentage: a January 2026 government announcement on piloting mobile-money salary payments for civil servants in unbanked areas; a 2025 World Bank-supported biometric civil servant registry (118,000 cards issued) intended to precede future payroll-system digitisation (SIGRH-Paie); and a 2025 public financial management digitisation programme (LOGIRAD, SIGeFiP, targeted for 2027) covering tax and customs. Historical IMF commentary notes a 'bancarisation' policy since 2011 requiring civil-service salaries to be paid via bank accounts, but does not quantify current digitised share. No source gives an actual percentage of government payments made digitally, so Unknown is confirmed rather than guessed.
